evidence.label: Determination of a metric and a unitary connection from one boundary patch
Smooth anisotropic uniqueness in the Calderón problem from one boundary patch
Nonuniqueness for bounded measurable scalar conductivities in three dimensions

headline: Claims one boundary patch determines a smooth metric; proves rough 3D conductivities can share all boundary data.
scope: Smooth metrics, and unitary rank-two connections, on compact manifolds of dimension at least three, measured on one boundary patch. Also rough scalar conductivities on a ball in ℝ³.
plain: Calderón's problem asks whether electrical measurements at the surface of a body determine what is inside. Two papers claim that, for smooth unknowns in dimension three or more, measurements on any small patch of the surface suffice, up to unavoidable relabelling. One handles a curved metric alone, the other a metric and a connection together. A third paper proves the opposite for rough conductivities: two different ones on a three-dimensional ball give exactly the same surface data. Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of this third result only.
doesNot: This does not give a way to reconstruct the interior from data, or a stability estimate. The smooth uniqueness results are not in the Lean scope, and the rough counterexample is in dimension three only.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Alberto Calderón, the inverse conductivity problem
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to settle smooth anisotropic Calderón uniqueness from one patch, and gives a Lean-checked rough counterexample in three dimensions.

explanation:
Start with a rod of length 1 that conducts electricity. Its conductivity γ may vary along it. The resistance from end to end is the integral of 1/γ. If γ = 1 everywhere, the resistance is 1. Now let γ = 2 on the first half and 2/3 on the second half. The resistance is (1/2)(1/2) + (1/2)(3/2) = 0.25 + 0.75 = 1 again. The two rods look the same from the ends. In one dimension, end measurements cannot see inside. The question is whether surface measurements can in three dimensions or more.

Calderón's problem asks whether the boundary response to every applied voltage determines the conductivity inside[2]. For smooth scalar conductivities in dimension at least three, Sylvester and Uhlmann proved uniqueness[3]. In the anisotropic version the unknown is a metric, a rule for lengths that can differ by direction. Then a change of interior coordinates that fixes the boundary cannot be detected. That ambiguity is unavoidable[4].

The second paper claims that this is the only ambiguity. A smooth metric in dimension at least three is determined, up to such a change of coordinates, from one boundary patch[5]. Voltages are applied and currents read on the same patch. It claims to resolve the smooth anisotropic problem with these same-patch measurements[6]. The first paper claims the same with a second unknown, a unitary connection on a rank-two bundle. A connection is a rule for carrying two-component complex values from point to point. The metric and connection are determined up to a coordinate change and a gauge change that fix the patch[1].

The third paper goes the other way for rough data. It builds two scalar conductivities on a ball of radius 3 in ℝ³. Both are bounded above and below by positive constants, and both equal 1 near the boundary. They differ on a set of positive volume, yet give the same full boundary response[7]. So uniqueness fails when only bounded measurability is assumed, already in dimension three[8]. Earlier results needed derivatives: Caro and Rogers proved uniqueness for Lipschitz conductivities in every dimension from three up[9]. The construction nests scaled copies of a small block with boundary tori[10]. This design hides an interior change from every boundary voltage.

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the rough three-dimensional counterexample. So that result is proved, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. The two smooth uniqueness results are not in the Lean scope and remain claims. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major if the smooth uniqueness proofs hold: they would settle a central inverse problem with one-patch data. Only the rough counterexample has a Lean statement. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: How easily electric current flows through a material at each point.
The rule that takes voltages applied on the boundary to the currents that flow out there.
Behaving differently in different directions, so the unknown is a metric rather than one number per point.
An open piece of the surface, possibly small, where voltages are applied and currents read.
A rule for carrying vector values from one point to a nearby point.
A change of reference frame at each point that does not change anything measurable.
